title: Where the tiller tills
hook: leave your chanting and beads; he is there where the tiller tills the hard ground (Gitanjali 11)
tomorrow: what did Tagore hand back to the British Crown, and why?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: made endless. The frail vessel, emptied and filled again with fresh life. Today, where Tagore says that filling actually happens, and it isn't where you'd expect.

The person who cleans the office after everyone leaves doesn't usually make the team photo. Tagore spent years watching people like that. His father sent him to manage the family's country estates in East Bengal, and he lived for long stretches on a houseboat on the river Padma, writing letters home about the farmers, boatmen and ferry crowds he saw from the deck. Then came Gitanjali's eleventh song, and it opens with an order.
screen: `NOT IN THE TEAM PHOTO.` → `A HOUSEBOAT ON THE PADMA.` → `THE SONG OPENS WITH AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then the answer: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." The song goes on: he's with them in sun and in shower, his garment covered with dust, so put off your holy cloak and come down on the dusty soil. It sounds like an attack on prayer. It isn't. Gitanjali is a book of prayers, and this song is one. The teaching is about where God lives. The God of the Upanishads that Tagore grew up with fills everything, and Gitanjali adds that this God has gladly taken on the bonds of creation and is bound up with us. A God like that can't be kept behind a temple's shut doors. So the holiest place in this song is a field at noon, and the worshipers are a farmer and a road crew. Tagore acted on it, too. Near his school he started Sriniketan, a center for rebuilding village life: farming, crafts, health. Honoring workers, in this song, isn't charity, and it isn't only good manners. It's going where God already is, out on the hard ground, sweating in the sun.
screen: `LEAVE THE SHUT TEMPLE.` · `THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.` · `GOD TOOK ON THE BONDS OF CREATION.` · `SRINIKETAN: VILLAGE LIFE REBUILT.` · then, large: `WHERE THE TILLER TILLS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose work you depended on today and probably never saw: whoever grew your rice, drove the truck, cleaned the floor. For two minutes, hold them in mind the way Tagore did, as the place where God is standing. If you know their name, say it quietly.
Where the tiller tills: Gitanjali's eleventh song, which sends the worshiper out of the shut temple to find God in the field and the dust of work.
Your line: where the tiller tills. The song moves God out of the shut room and onto the hard ground. Talk tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Gitanjali often take song 11 as a call to find God in work and among workers; Tagore's own Sriniketan center, near Santiniketan, worked on farming, crafts and village health.
